In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of polypharmacy prediction models, exploring their performance on multiple tasks and evaluating the impact of labeling strategies. Our findings suggest that labeling strategies have a substantial effect on model performance, with supervised learning outperforming semi-supervised and unsupervised methods. Notably, we observed that even with extensive unlabeled data, the performance of semi-supervised learning models did not significantly improve compared to supervised learning. Our results also indicate that the performance of models varies greatly depending on the task, with some achieving high accuracy and others struggling with low precision. To facilitate further research, we make our code and labeling strategies publicly available.

This paper introduces an Itô-Wentzell type formula tailored to paths with α-Hölder regularity of $\alpha$ in the interval $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}]$. The formula is applicable to functions with rough derivatives in a Sobolev space of index $s$ where $s$ is in the interval $\left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$. The formula is significant as it connects the solution of a rough differential equation to its driver and initial condition, enabling the solution to be represented as an integral of the differential of the rough driver along a path defined by the differential of the Brownian motion. The formula is also instrumental in proving the uniqueness of solutions to rough differential equations with rough drivers.

In a decentralized learning environment, a notable issue with data distribution is heterogeneity. This problem is particularly pronounced in image classification tasks, where data is often fragmented among nodes with different labels. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a new method for supervised learning in a heterogeneous environment. The proposed approach involves creating a new loss function that takes into account the differences in data labels. This is achieved by utilizing a parameterized form of the Kullback-Leibler divergence to derive a federated learning objective function. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.

We investigate the development of turbulence in a rotating system using the Shakura and Stepinski model, and find that its dynamics can be accurately described by an infinite number of interacting wave triads. This result allows us to distinguish the turbulence in this system from the geostrophic turbulence characterized by large-scale vortices, by showing that the Shakura and Stepinski model's spectrum is more consistent with a universal scaling found in wave turbulence.

This study investigates the relationship between court-ordered mental health treatment and recidivism among offenders on probation. Utilizing a large dataset from the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education, we employ statistical analysis to control for relevant factors and minimize bias. Our results indicate that receiving mental health treatment through the courts significantly reduces the likelihood of offenders returning to the justice system within five years. Notably, this effect is most pronounced among those with prior convictions, for whom the risk of recidivism is cut in half.

A prevalent challenge in medical image analysis is the segmentation of complex structures from heterogeneous images. This task is complicated by the need for detailed pixel-level annotations, which are time-consuming and costly to obtain. To address this issue, we propose a novel self-supervised medical image segmentation framework, which leverages unlabelled data to learn segmentation tasks. By establishing a correspondence graph between image patches based on local contextual cues and a global anatomical template, our method learns to segment images by reconstructing this template. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to cardiac MR image segmentation and achieving comparable results to supervised methods on two public datasets.

The Large Hadron Collider's Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector at CERN will undergo a significant upgrade to enhance its precision in search for new physics beyond the Standard Model. As part of this upgrade, the CMS detector's jet identification system will be improved to accurately distinguish between quark and gluon jets. This paper outlines the design of the upgraded jet identification system, which incorporates advanced machine learning algorithms and utilizes detailed simulations to evaluate its performance. By implementing a sophisticated neural network, we achieved a 50% increase in separating quark and gluon jets, reducing the misidentification rate of quark jets to less than 10% and achieving a 90% identification rate for gluon jets. Furthermore, this system demonstrated robustness in handling various background conditions and was found to be effective in distinguishing light-quark and heavy-quark jets.

This paper introduces ArtNet, a novel neural rendering framework that utilizes
articulated models for creating realistic virtual human avatars. By leveraging
neural radiance fields and articulated kinematic chains, ArtNet enables real-time
rendering of complex character animations while eliminating the need for time-consuming
animation culling and texture mapping. In particular, ArtNet enables dynamic
skinning, automatic texture mapping, and real-time rendering of detailed characters.
Our results demonstrate that ArtNet achieves high visual fidelity with minimal
computational overhead.

Understanding how local atomic disorder affects materials performance and durability is crucial for optimizing their properties and extending their lifespan.  A novel approach to this challenge is presented through a method that leverages machine learning and atomic resolution imaging to map local environments and their impact on material properties.  This approach is successfully applied to the study of grain boundaries in two materials: yttria, a critical component in nuclear fuel, and indium antimonide, a semiconductor with high electron mobility.  The results reveal that a grain boundary in yttria has a high defect density and radioactivity, while in indium antimonide, a specific grain boundary exhibits high electron mobility and surface recombination.  The analysis of these findings provides new insights into the structure-property relationship of these materials and demonstrates the potential of this approach for identifying and evaluating the performance of materials at the atomic level.

This research paper proposes a new method for estimating parameters in a mixture of two exponential distributions with unknown means. The proposed method involves Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) that account for the mixing distribution's uncertainty. The study evaluates the performance of these estimators through simulations and compares them to traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimators (MLE). The results show that the bias and mean squared error of the GMLE are significantly lower than those of the MLE, especially when the mixing proportion is small.

Knowledge tracing models have been highly effective in predicting students' future performance and underlying knowledge states. However, these models are typically trained on isolated questions within educational platforms, discarding valuable contextual information. In contrast, real-world assessments like essays and discussions provide rich contextual data that can significantly influence test scores. We argue that knowledge tracing should also account for contextual factors to provide a holistic understanding of students' knowledge and learning processes. To achieve this, we propose Context-Aware Knowledge Tracing (CAKT), a novel framework that incorporates contextual information from multi-modal data. CAKT's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study on scoring essay responses within a physics course, utilizing both visual descriptions and essay content to inform assessments. The results show that CAKT outperforms baseline models, successfully leveraging contextual data to capture learning behaviors and accurately predict student performance.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. If the manifold $M$ does not comprise any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

The veriT solver has been a prominent SMT competitor in recent evaluations, with veriT consistently ranking high in benchmarks across various categories. veriT's success can be attributed to its user base, comprising leading verification and theorem proving systems, including Coq, Isabelle/HOL, and MathSAT5. These tools have contributed to veriT's development by providing valuable feedback and guiding its development towards practical applications. In this paper, we provide an overview of the veriT solver, its architecture, and proof representation. We also discuss the benefits of using veriT's proof format, particularly its ability to convey uncertainty through set-theoretic interpretations. Furthermore, we outline the solver's performance in the 2020 SMT competition and present a comparison with other SMT solvers.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates becomes less efficient. This study investigates the impact of a large number of participating devices and explores ways to enhance scalability. We propose a new aggregation method called 'robust federated learning' and demonstrate its effectiveness in overcoming update synchronization issues. Theoretical analysis and experimental results show that this approach can achieve high accuracy even with a large number of devices.

A new alphabet called the "phoneme alphabet" has been proposed for use in automatic speech recognition systems. This alphabet is derived from the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and is more compact than the IPA, with 46 units instead of 107. The IPA is typically used for ASR systems, but it is a large and complex system that can be difficult to train. In contrast, the phoneme alphabet is more balanced and has a more even distribution of units, with 10 units for vowels and 36 for consonants. This balance is thought to be beneficial for training ASR systems. Experiments were conducted to compare the performance of ASR systems trained on the IPA and the phoneme alphabet, using the TIMIT dataset. The results showed that the phoneme alphabet resulted in a 10% reduction in error rate compared to the IPA.

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Gamers, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Twitch Gamers as a test bed for social network datasets.

Researchers have long been fascinated by the enigmatic $K^0\bar{K^0}$ decay mode, specifically the di-pion or di-kaon system, which has yielded an unexplained state in previous studies. A recent experiment at the J-PET facility utilized a 12.4 GeV electron beam to produce the desired reaction and detect the resulting particles. By analyzing 1.2 x 10^11 electron interactions with the detector material, the researchers identified 1.3 x 10^6 $K^0\bar{K^0}$ events with a specific energy spectrum. A new analysis of the di-kaon system revealed a narrow resonance at 1751.87 MeV with 4.2 MeV width, which is likely the $\phi(1680)$ meson. By subtracting the $\phi(1680)$ contribution from the data, a new peak emerged at 1720.33 MeV with 5.9 MeV width, which could be the long-sought $f_0(1750)$ resonance. Furthermore, by analyzing the di-pion system, the researchers found a narrow peak at 1680.34 MeV with 2.5 MeV width, which is consistent with the $\phi(1680)$ meson, and a broader peak at 1720.33 MeV with 5.9 MeV width, which could be the $f_0(1750

We investigate the impact of a fifth dimension on Hawking radiation from black holes and find that it can be accounted for by modifying the surface gravity in accordance with the universal gravitation formula. This leads to a change in the temperature and energy spectrum of the radiation, ultimately resulting in a decrease in the information paradox. The associated timescale for the radiation's decline also changes with the presence of the extra dimension.

This research paper presents a novel force sensor simulation method called the transmission force observer (TFOB) for series elastic actuators (SEAs). The traditional approach to estimating SEA forces involves complex algorithms and expensive sensors. In contrast, the TFOB method leverages a simple mathematical model to estimate the transmission dynamics and the elastic element's behavior, allowing for the simulation of the force sensor's response. By incorporating the actual measurement data from the SEA's transmission, the TFOB model can accurately predict the sensor's output, thereby enabling force control. The proposed method was implemented on a practical SEA testbed and demonstrated to achieve precise force control, outperforming the actual force sensor in a comparison test.

A floating raft of particles offers a clear model for studying material breakdown. The mechanism of failure is complex and influenced by various factors, including the rate of expansion, the presence of defects, and the raft's initial conditions. In this study, we examine the morphology of failure in a particle raft that is expanding at a constant rate and find that it transitions from a uniform pattern of cracks to a more disordered pattern as the expansion rate increases. The transition occurs suddenly, and we identify the critical point by analyzing the stress distribution and the formation of cracks. The size of the critical point shows a power-law relationship with the viscosity of the surrounding fluid, and we propose that it represents a universal point of instability.

We have examined SU(Nc) gauge theories in three-dimensional space on a lattice, with the presence of multi-component scalar fields that adhere to the fundamental and anti-fundamental symmetry properties of SU(Nc). The study focused on a specific scalar field configuration, where a quartic potential is present to stabilize the scalar field's behavior. The lattice was utilized to simulate the scalar field's thermodynamic properties, with the application of Monte Carlo methods to determine the scalar field's energy density at various temperatures. The results revealed that the energy density exhibits a distinct peak value at a specific temperature, which is influenced by the scalar field's mass and the SU(Nc) gauge group's rank. The study also explored the peak's location and magnitude as a function of the scalar field's mass and the SU(Nc) gauge group's rank.

This paper introduces a novel TD learning approach for marine navigation, utilizing Gaussian Process regression to enhance policy updates.  By leveraging the predictive power of GP in modeling underwater sensor data and robot dynamics, we've developed a TD learning algorithm that adapts to the challenges of underwater environments.  Our method's benefits are demonstrated through simulations of a robot learning to navigate by observing changes in water temperature, and the results show it outperforms traditional TD learning and GP-based policy optimization.

This research focuses on developing sorting networks with comparators of a specific arity, $d$, for a variable number of inputs, $n$. We are particularly interested in $d \geq \log_2 n$, as this would allow us to sort $n$-bit strings using only $\log_2 n$-sized sorting networks. Our main achievement is establishing a lower bound for the depth of such sorting networks, $D$, in terms of $d$ and $n$. This lower bound is more precise than any previous lower bound and holds true for $d \geq \log_2 n$. We also developed a sorting network with a depth of $D+1$ for $d = \log_2 n$. Furthermore, we investigated the case where $d$ is a constant and found that there are constant-depth sorting networks for this scenario.

We have derived a set of relativistic and anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in allometric form, which describe the relationships between mass, radius, and specific potential in a spherically symmetric, self-gravitating system. These equations are unique in that they don't require any additional parameters beyond those defining the mass function and the exponent in the radial component. We have also an analytically solved an anisotropic star problem using the'mass-radius' relation, which shows that the anisotropic 'NUT' solution satisfies this condition when a particular allometric form is applied.

Using a new technique to model the response of a galaxy to a perturbing force, we've developed a highly detailed and realistic model of the Milky Way. This model, which includes a bar at the center and a massive bulge, was subjected to various tests to ensure its accuracy. We then used it to study the galaxy's normal modes of oscillation and how they affect its rotation curves. Our analysis revealed that a specific mode of oscillation, which creates a spiral wave pattern, has a significant impact on the rotation curve in the inner region of the galaxy. However, when we accounted for the effects of this mode on the rotation curve, it matched the observed values very closely, with a small discrepancy only in the outer regions. Notably, we found that a bar is essential for producing the observed rotation curve in the galaxy's central region.

Galactic mergers play a significant role in shaping galaxy evolution, particularly in how they affect galaxy morphology. The Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 has provided high-resolution images of galaxies in the Hubble Deep Field-South, allowing researchers to study the impact of major mergers on galaxy morphology. By analyzing these images, researchers found that mergers have a lasting impact on galaxy morphology, with 30% of galaxies showing signs of irregular morphology up to 1 billion years after a major merger. However, the influence of mergers on galaxy morphology decreases over time, with only 10% of galaxies exhibiting irregular morphology more than 1 billion years after a major merger. The study also found that the spin of galaxies is affected by mergers, with a significant decrease in spin rates up to 1 billion years after a major merger. However, the influence of mergers on galaxy spin rates is less pronounced over time, with only a slight decrease in spin rates more than 1 billion years after a major merger. The study also found that the mass of the central black hole in galaxies is directly proportional to the mass of the galaxy's bulge, with a ratio of 0.0003. The study also found that the mass of the central black hole in galaxies is directly proportional to the mass of the galaxy's spin rate, with a ratio of 0.00002. This paper presents a cutting-edge, multi-class COVID-19 severity detection system that utilizes chest CT images to identify four different grades of severity: mild, moderate, severe, and non-COVID-19 cases. By leveraging a novel, hierarchical classification network that combines attention mechanisms and dense connectivity, our system achieves exceptional performance on two prominent datasets, outperforming existing methods and demonstrating robustness in real-world applications.

This study proposes a meta-learning method for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) to adapt to new domains with only a few examples. By leveraging the similarities between natural language and mathematics, we frame GEC as a problem of learning to solve label-related equations for sentence transformations. We develop a task-aware approach to optimize a general learning algorithm, allowing for efficient updates during few-shot adaptation. The proposed method is evaluated on the WASSA 2015 GEC task, achieving a significant 10.56% gain in F-score when adapting to new domains from only four examples.

Rounding is a common technique used in data collection, particularly when gathering information on count variables. This study focuses on understanding how data is affected when a non-negative discrete random variable is rounded to the nearest ten, and then analyzed through the lens of a related continuous random variable. We derive the distribution of the rounded variable in terms of its original form, and explore specific cases involving binomial and Poisson distributions. Additionally, we discuss the implications of rounding on the central limit theorem and establish the asymptotic distribution of the rounded variable as it approaches normality.

We have investigated the magnetic properties of the cubic GdInO$_3$ single crystal through direct and inverse Raman spectroscopy.  Our analysis reveals two distinct antiferromagnetic phase transitions in GdInO$_3$, occurring at 4.5 K and 2.5 K, respectively.  By utilizing a microscopic model, we were able to simulate the Raman spectra and determine the local magnetic moments' orientation in each phase.  Furthermore, we found that the 4.5 K phase transition temperature aligns with the expected value based on the crystal's lattice parameters.

The concept of allocating goods among self-interested agents, specifically in the context of allocating digital goods, has been extensively studied in the field of algorithmic game theory. Envy-free allocation mechanisms, which eliminate envy among agents, are highly sought after. However, achieving perfect envy-free allocation for all agents is often impractical due to the high computational requirements. As a result, researchers have been exploring alternative concepts, such as allocating one good (EF1) or defining specific boundaries for allowed envy (e.g., bounded by epsilon, EF-epsilon), in order to balance fairness with computational efficiency. In this study, we focus on the selfless digital good exchange (SGX) model, which allows agents to exchange goods without knowing each other's identities. We introduce a new concept, envy-free up to two goods (EF2), and demonstrate that it is computationally unfeasible to design mechanisms that achieve this level of fairness for all agents. However, we do show that achieving EF1 is computationally possible. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the computational requirements in achieving EF1 in certain exchange scenarios.

In this research, we propose a novel approach to unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) using stochastic translation. Our method leverages the advantages of approximate inference in domain adaptation, as we demonstrate that approximating the mutual information between source and target data through stochastic source-to-target translations yields an optimized solution. Specifically, we show that using non-parametric reordering (i.e., reversing the order of mean and log) leads to an upper bound for the estimated mutual information. By applying this reordering to a simple reordering-based estimator, we derive a more effective estimator that outperforms current state-of-the-art UDA methods. Our proposed method is flexible and can be integrated with various stochastic translation models, including sequence-to-sequence translators. We validate the efficacy of our approach through comprehensive experiments on three UDA tasks, including unsupervised domain adaptation and multi-domain adaptation, which yield superior results compared to existing methods.

UGC 8839, a faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation in its outer regions, which is an uncommon feature among similar spiral galaxies. Researchers propose that the unusual, high-rate star formation observed in the galaxy's outermost regions is a result of the gravitational influence of a massive, low-luminosity companion galaxy, which is positioned at a significant angle relative to the line of sight. The interaction between these two galaxies is believed to have triggered the outer star formation in UGC 8839. The study of UGC 8839 provides valuable insights into the effects of gravitational tidal forces on the structure of spiral galaxies, particularly in situations where the gravitational pull of a massive companion galaxy is not directly observable.

Researchers are exploring the possibility of detecting dark matter through the observation of rare nuclear recoil events in highly sensitive detectors. A new approach, known as paleo-detection, involves analyzing ancient samples for signs of dark matter interaction, which could potentially offer a more effective method of detection. By utilizing existing artifacts and analyzing them for the characteristic signatures of dark matter, paleo-detection may be able to surpass conventional detection methods in terms of sensitivity and time of observation. However, this approach faces significant challenges in achieving a suitable dark matter signature and distinguishing it from other phenomena, such as radioactive contamination. Nevertheless, paleo-detection could potentially provide a more efficient and cost-effective means of dark matter detection.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, building on the existing work of DP-Dazuko and DP-Select. Furthermore, the proposed DP-Sync is showcased to provide efficient update pattern protection, leveraging the properties of differential privacy through threshold-based data updates.

The integration of Machine Learning in security-sensitive areas like national defense and finance is being hindered by the lack of transparency in its decision-making processes. This study proposes a novel method for analyzing the predictability of Artificial Neural Network-based classification models, which can effectively gauge the trustworthiness of their outputs. By utilizing a specially designed training dataset, the research demonstrates that the proposed method is both feasible and reliable. The results show that the degree of output reliability is inversely proportional to the model's complexity and the presence of noise in the training data. Furthermore, the research reveals that the proposed method can accurately predict the output reliability for both linear and non-linear models, and that the degree of this reliability varies linearly with the model's input magnitude. The study also finds that the proposed method can detect output errors caused by adversarial attacks, and that the degree of this error is proportional to the model's complexity and the magnitude of the input.

Minimally invasive surgery, a highly effective treatment with fewer complications, is widely adopted in various medical fields. However, its application is limited due to high costs and the need for advanced equipment. To make it more accessible, this study proposes a novel approach using a convolutional neural network (CNN) for automated laparoscopic image enhancement from a single endoscopic image. The proposed method utilizes a U-Net architecture, specifically designed for retinopathy detection, and trains the network with a limited dataset of laparoscopic images. Experimental results show that the proposed system can effectively enhance images and perform tasks such as detecting tumors and blood vessels. Notably, the algorithm can convert a single endoscopic image into a composite image consisting of a magnified detail area and a blood vessel map, thereby facilitating real-time surgical assistance.

This paper introduces a novel approach called large-scale unlabeled surveillance video exploration (LUSE), which leverages vast amounts of unlabeled surveillance footage for person re-identification. By developing a method to explore and learn from these videos without labels, LUSE enables the discovery of new re-identification models that excel in real-world scenarios. Our framework consists of two primary components: a video exploration technique and a person re-identification model that learns from the discovered data. In our experiments, LUSE outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on the MSMTL and DukeMTMC-RFW datasets, achieving a rank-1 accuracy of 44.4% and 24.2% respectively, with a mean accuracy of 44.1% and 30.4% respectively.

This research introduces a new model that builds on the CAPM by incorporating a unique type of threshold-based relationship between expected returns and wealth. The model's equation is inspired by the Probit model, but includes a key modification that prevents it from becoming singular. We demonstrate that this revised equation can be represented in a linear form similar to the CAPM, making it estimable with conventional linear regression tools. Additionally, we show that this linear representation can be used to estimate the model's parameters. Furthermore, we propose a method to determine the optimal wealth threshold based on a specific error measure. We apply this model to analyze the S&P 500 index and identify a significant non-linear relationship between expected returns and wealth.

Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, improved data from the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array is expected to yield significant results in the near future. This study presents a novel, model-independent technique for detecting the gravitational wave background through the combination of multiple pulsar pairs. The technique leverages the unique properties of pulsar data to achieve a factor of two improvement in sensitivity compared to traditional methods. When applied to the PPTA data set, this technique is expected to reveal the gravitational wave background signal, assuming its amplitude is greater than 4.5 x 10^-14 Hu units at a 95% confidence level.

This study examines the quark structure of the pion, specifically within the context of the bound state of quarks and its correlation function. Correlation functions of quark currents within a quantum chromodynamics simulation are analyzed to determine the quark structure of the pion. The analysis focuses on correlation functions of two quark currents that share the same momentum, one with a scalar and the other with a vector structure. The correlation functions are then used to derive the quark structure of the pion, taking into account the contribution of a ghost field that arises from the quantum chromodynamics gauge field. The study compares the quark structure of the pion derived from correlation functions of the shared momentum quark currents with the quark structure obtained from a quantum chromodynamics calculation of the quark propagator difference. The quark structure of the pion is found to be independent of the momentum at low energies, in line with chiral perturbation theory predictions.

The mass accretion process in protoplanetary disks around young stars is influenced by several factors, including magnetic fields, disk properties, and stellar mass. To better understand this process, researchers have been using observations of stellar masses, disk growth, and mass accretion to create a database of 20 stars with similar ages and masses. This study aims to investigate how mass accretion rates vary with stellar mass and disk growth rates, and to explore the presence of distinct classes of behavior in the mass accretion process. By analyzing the data, the researchers found that mass accretion rates are directly proportional to stellar mass, and that the relationship between mass accretion rates and disk growth rates follows a power-law with an index of 0.45. Furthermore, the study suggests that the mass accretion process in protoplanetary disks can be described by a self-regulated mechanism that maintains a balance between mass accretion and disk growth, and that the process exhibits a characteristic timescale of 0.1-1 Myr.

This research investigates the connection between luck, inequality, and income redistribution.
It presents a public goods game that allows participants to observe the outcomes of luck-dependent worker tasks and then makes them decide on redistribution.
The findings indicate that people generally choose to redistribute more when inequality is caused by luck rather than skill.
However, this preference for luck-based inequality over skill-based inequality is not consistently observed and depends on the level of free riding in the game.
A theoretical model explains the relationship between luck, inequality, and redistribution, highlighting the role of perceived luck and its impact on redistribution.
The model also explores how the level of redistribution is affected by the level of free riding and the perceived luck involved.

Let's consider the space of partial flags in a vector space, denoted as P, and a map $\pi: X \to Y$ between two spaces of partial flags. We're interested in studying the closed subvarieties of Schubert cells in X that correspond to maps from X to Y that factor through P. These subvarieties are closely related to the maps from X to Y that factor through P and can be analyzed using the geometry of Schubert varieties. In this paper, we'll investigate the subvarieties of maps from X to Y that factor through P and use this to derive formulas for the cohomology classes of these subvarieties.

In machine learning, a model's performance is often evaluated by a quality metric that depends on relevant data. Unsupervised learning algorithms have been developed to estimate the importance of data points to this performance metric during model training. These algorithms can be used to identify and remove influential data points, helping to address issues like data quality improvement and robustness. By applying the concept of Shapley values to machine learning, we can compute the value of each data point for model training, even when models are trained using stochastic methods. We show that the standard approach to computing Shapley values is not applicable to machine learning, but a new algorithm can estimate the value of each data point when models are trained using stochastic gradient descent. This algorithm is efficient and accurate, outperforming existing methods on several benchmark datasets.

We've conducted a comprehensive radio survey of 85 Galactic globular clusters using the VLA and ATCA, resulting in detailed source counts within these clusters. These observations reveal a notable correlation between radio sources within globular clusters and their encounter rates during formation, with higher encounter rates associated with more radio sources. Specifically, we found that the density of radio sources is greater in globular clusters with encounter rates above 0.1 pc$^{-3}$ myr$^{-1}$, and that there's a notable increase in the number of low-luminosity radio sources at higher encounter rates. These findings suggest that the growth of low-luminosity radio sources is linked to the collision of stars with compact remnants, and that the collision rate plays a significant role in determining the radio source population within these clusters.

Complex systems, including social networks, transportation systems, and biological webs, are often inaccurately represented as graphs, which can lead to significant errors in modeling and analysis. Hypergraphs provide a more precise and flexible framework for capturing these interactions by linking multiple nodes to each other. However, the limited availability of real-world hypergraph data and the computational challenges of analyzing them have hindered their use. In this study, we present a novel method for generating hypergraphs in an evolving and dynamic environment, leveraging a degree sequence that reflects the past state of the system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using both synthetic and real-world data, including a scientific collaboration network, and show that it can accurately reproduce the distribution of degrees and the structure of past snapshots. Furthermore, we found that this method outperforms existing hypergraph generation methods and can identify and remove malicious nodes with high accuracy.

We introduce a concept of conditional entropy to quantify the asymmetry of spontaneous emission spectra from microcavity lasers. Calculations for different emission directions are performed, and the results show that higher entropy values correspond to more directional emission. The relationship between entropy and directivity is explored, and the impact of photon density on entropy is examined through experimental light pattern measurements and numerical simulations.

We studied the spatial distribution of atoms within a heated alkali-metal vapor, observing how it changes with temperature, distance from the source, and the wavelength of light used to probe it. By analyzing the effects of temperature on the spread of atomic positions, we found it increases linearly with temperature and potentially influences the coherence properties of light. Furthermore, we found that the distance over which the distribution of atoms changes significantly is comparable to the coherence length, which is influenced by the temperature and the wavelength of light. This understanding is critical for optimizing the performance of coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy in highly scattering environments.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Offline learning
occurs in a setting where an entire dataset is collected beforehand, and the
goal is to train multiple interacting agents using this data without further
exploration. The primary challenge in offline learning is that the performance
of individual agents may not contribute to optimal team outcomes, as the teams'
outcomes are interdependent. To tackle this issue, we propose a new offline
learning approach called Adversarial Interdependent Critic (AIC), which uses
an adversary to evaluate the connection between individual actions and the team's
outcomes. The proposed method, Adversarial Interdependent Critic, is a general
framework for offline learning that can be applied to various multi-agent
scenarios. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on
two complex datasets, including the MultiWorld dataset and the CarLa dataset,
which show that the proposed method outperforms existing offline learning
techniques by a significant margin of 20-30%.

This study proposes a novel approach for registering MV images taken during radiation therapy, which utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a coarse-to-fine optimization technique. Traditional image registration methods have been successful but often rely on expensive computational processes and assume that low-resolution images can accurately represent the initial patient anatomy. In contrast, our proposed framework leverages a CNN to generate high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs and utilizes a coarse-to-fine optimization algorithm to refine the results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a dataset of pelvic MV images and comparing it to two other methods, including a popular deep learning technique and a traditional image registration algorithm. Our results show that our proposed framework achieves the best performance, with a mean surface distance of 1.83 mm, outperforming the other methods with a mean surface distance of 2.01 mm and 2.23 mm respectively.

In 1927, Einstein used an experiment involving a beam splitter to challenge the completeness of quantum mechanics, famously leading Bohr to respond with the principle of complementarity. However, examining this scenario through instantaneous nonlocal effects offers a more straightforward explanation for the issue. We find that, in order for quantum mechanics to be considered a local hidden variable theory, its description of correlations must be at least as nontrivial as $|\psi\rangle|\phi\rab$. Furthermore, this condition leads to a completeness criterion for quantum mechanics, which is met by both pure and mixed states. Additionally, we demonstrate that the nontriviality of $|\psi\rab|\phi\rab$ is essential for describing instantaneous nonlocal effects, which can be utilized to create superluminal communication. Consequently, this shows that the incompleteness of quantum mechanics, as demonstrated by Einstein's thought experiment, is a genuine manifestation of the speed limit in quantum mechanics.

The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) relies heavily on IoV data, which holds significant value, but also poses a risk to privacy and security. As IoV technology advances, there is a growing need for secure and efficient data sharing. This paper introduces a novel Federated Learning (FL) framework, which enables secure and efficient data sharing for IoV applications. By utilizing homomorphic encryption and multi-party computation, this framework protects user privacy while facilitating collaborative learning. The proposed framework is evaluated for its performance and energy efficiency, demonstrating its potential for safeguarding IoV data privacy and security.

We've conducted a thorough examination of the 2016 FRODOSpec and Skye spectra of the nova V392 Persei, covering the period from 2016 August 17 to 2017 August 24, and gathered additional data from the Strömgren-Spectroscopic Survey for a Solar-like Anchor (S4N) Nova database. Our analysis of the spectra revealed that the nova's spectral characteristics evolved from a hot, blue spectrum to a cooler, redder spectrum, and eventually to a spectrum with a temperature similar to that of the central star. We've also observed the emergence of broad absorption lines in the spectra, which can be attributed to the presence of a massive outflow with velocities ranging from 2000 to 4000 km/s. Our examination of the spectral data also showed that the nova's spectral energy distribution changed from a power-law index of 1.5 to 0.5 over time, and that the absorption lines became broader and more pronounced as the nova's temperature decreased. Notably, the decline time of V392 Persei in the V-band was significantly longer than average, taking around 140 days, and its post-eruption brightness remained elevated for an extended period.

Achieving reliable and efficient quantum computing requires addressing the issue of quantum errors through the use of error correction codes. Implementing code operations with multi-qubit gates improves fault tolerance by reducing the impact of individual gate failures. This work presents a method to optimize the generation of stabilizer states for any code by combining available multi-qubit gates, thus enabling the effective use of any-qubit gates within a quantum circuit. This approach is particularly beneficial for codes that require multiple any-qubit gates, such as the Shor code, and demonstrates its application with a five-qubit code. The proposed technique offers improved fault tolerance and efficient generation of stabilizer states, which can serve as resource states for quantum computation.

A proposed codebook construction method utilizes Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks for downlink transmission in multiuser systems. This approach generates codebooks by creating a set of basis vectors from a small number of training sequences at the receiver, which are then combined to form the codebook. The codebook is optimized to minimize the worst-case distortion when transmitting data from a limited number of sources. It is shown that the optimal codebook can be achieved by selecting the most relevant components from a trained GMM, and that this approach outperforms traditional random codebook construction. The performance of this method is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing distortion and improving spectral efficiency.

The study of a two-dimensional, robust crosscurrent on a three-dimensional lattice reveals that it can withstand certain types of disorder, including vacancies and bond dilution, provided that the impurities are sufficiently sparse. Notably, the crosscurrent remains stable under conditions where the lattice's connectivity is high, specifically above the percolation threshold. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the crosscurrent's thermal fluctuations follow a power-law behavior, characterized by a diverging thermal length scale as the chemical potential is adjusted to optimize the crosscurrent's amplitude. The crosscurrent's spatial patterns are found to be influenced by the chemical potential, resulting in a transition from localized inclusions to a more complex, long-range arrangement as the chemical potential increases.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research has determined the maximum rate of change of Bondi mass, typically denoted as M, and the rate of change of its square, M^2. In general relativity, the allowed rate of change of Bondi mass is proportional to the Planck mass to the fourth power. Interestingly, this proportionality also holds in $f(R)$ gravity theories. Furthermore, it has been found that the rate of change of the square of Bondi mass in Einstein gravity is directly proportional to the Planck mass to the fourth power, and this proportionality is also observed in the pure gravity theories associated with higher-dimensional branes in the context of the fundamental string theory. Notably, this proportionality is equivalent to Dyson's maximum luminosity, which is the maximum power at which a star can shine.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters and predict that approximately 0.1% of these remnants will merge at redshifts greater than 0. By modeling the evolution of nuclear star clusters, we find that they can host a significant number of Population III binary remnants with masses between 0.3-3.0 solar masses. These remnants are responsible for producing gravitational waves detectable by the Laser Interferometer Space Telescope through mergers of neutron star-black hole, black hole-binary black hole, and neutron star-neutron star systems. The detection rates for these events are estimated to be 0.17, 0.04, and 0.01 per year, respectively. The distribution of redshifts for these events peaks at 0.24, allowing for the possibility of observing Population III binary remnants through gravitational waves across a wide range of redshifts.

The Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is a space-based mission that will detect and observe high-energy counterparts to gravitational waves in the 0.1-1.0 MeV energy range. With two wide-field-of-view telescopes, GECAM will provide all-sky coverage and a detection sensitivity comparable to that of the Large Area Telescope on the Gamma-Ray Observatory. The onboard software will utilize real-time gravitational wave data from the Laser Interferometer gravitational wave observatory and Virgo to pinpoint and observe Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) within 10 seconds. The mission will also carry out a hard X-ray survey of the Galactic center and selected supernova remnants. The payload is designed to provide 100 kbps downlink capability, with a 1.5 m^2 deployment area and a mass of approximately 2500 kg. The launch is set for 2023 on a Long March 4B rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center.

This paper explores the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a semigroup {phi_t} to be invariant on these spaces, and this condition is expressed in terms of the behavior of the function phi(t) - t as t approaches 0. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the compact members of the semigroup, and this characterization leads to a conclusion about the compactness of the identity operator on BMOA_p for 1 <= p < 2.

The complex evolution of scientific disciplines can be understood through a model that considers the interplay between knowledge and productivity. This model posits that there exists a universal relationship between the amount of knowledge and productivity in a given scientific field, with productivity being a function of the amount of knowledge raised to a power that indicates the level of efficiency in the field. The model is supported by analyzing the citation patterns in physics from 1893 to 2010, and it is found that the efficiency in this time period decreased from 2 to 1.1, with a significant drop occurring in the last quarter of the 20th century. This decrease in efficiency is associated with a rise in low-productivity papers, which are defined as those cited fewer than 10 times, and it is found that the probability of a paper being highly cited (cited more than 10 times) decreased from 0.23 to 0.12 over this time period. The model also predicts that the number of highly cited papers will continue to decrease in the future, with a possible increase in the number of papers with zero citations.

This research focuses on a dual-hop OFDM wireless system with two users, where one user acts as a relay between the other two. We examine two scenarios: one where the relay uses all available subcarriers and another where the relay selects specific subcarriers for transmission. In both cases, we aim to maximize the overall secure data transfer rate while considering the limitations of each user's power and the characteristics of the wireless channel. For the first scenario, we develop an efficient algorithm to find the optimal solution, while for the second scenario, we design a suboptimal approach to tackle the problem. Additionally, we provide numerical examples and theoretical analysis to compare the performance of these strategies.

The number of chiral edge modes in two-dimensional topological systems corresponds to the difference in Chern numbers between a given system and its trivialized counterpart. This relationship holds even in the presence of multiple gaps, where distinct phases are separated by multiple regions of the spectrum that host topological edge modes. In this study, we demonstrate that a related two-dimensional photonic system also exhibits topological edge modes corresponding to the difference in Berry torque vectors between its own Chern numbers and those of a trivialized version. However, this relationship only applies to specific energy levels within the gap where the comparison is made.

The integration of automated vehicles into traffic systems is a promising development, but it also raises concerns about the increased risk of accidents caused by their connection to other vehicles during signal phases. To mitigate this risk, it's essential to develop strategies for automated vehicles to prioritize safety when interacting with human-driven vehicles at traffic lights. In this study, we focus on the scenario where an automated vehicle is approaching a traffic light and detects a human-driven vehicle in the adjacent lane, which is not responding to the impending red light. We propose a predictive control method that enables the automated vehicle to anticipate the human-driven vehicle's potential actions and adjust its speed to avoid a collision, minimizing braking time and reducing stop-and-go traffic. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through simulations, which show that it can significantly reduce braking frequency and duration by up to 30% and 50%, respectively, compared to traditional braking methods.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to evaluate virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, reasoning, and real-world skill execution. These games are typically described through simple descriptions, such as web pages or basic text, which agents must interpret to take appropriate actions. In this work, we present a comprehensive dataset, called TextWorld Dataset, comprising 24 diverse games that assess a range of practical abilities, including communication, navigation, and manual skills. Each game is paired with a corresponding text description, and the dataset is designed to facilitate the development of text-based agents by allowing them to learn from a wide range of tasks rather than being limited to a specific domain.

Deep learning models like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have achieved high accuracy in time series forecasting but are limited by their own complexity, hindering their deployment on resource-constrained devices. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel, compact LSTM architecture called the Intrinsic Gate LSTM (IG-LSTM) that significantly reduces model size while preserving high accuracy. The proposed IG-LSTM model utilizes an intrinsic gate to eliminate unnecessary computations and fuse gate operations, resulting in a substantial decrease in model parameters without sacrificing performance. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed IG-LSTM achieves superior forecasting accuracy and significantly lower model complexity compared to existing compact LSTM variants and traditional LSTM. Furthermore, the IG-LSTM exhibits excellent scalability on hardware, outperforming other compact LSTM models in inference efficiency.

Despite advancements in NLP through neural models, their deployment in resource-constrained environments remains a significant challenge. This issue is particularly pronounced in tasks like neural paraphrase detection, where the need for extensive labeled data and precise contextual understanding hinders progress. To address this, we propose a novel, highly efficient approach called Paraphrase Knowledge Graph Embedding with Neural Data Augmentation (PKGE-DA). This method leverages weak supervision from unpaired data and combines neural data augmentation with neural paraphrase detection to enhance model performance. By iteratively training a model on augmented data with increasing quality, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the Winograd Schema Challenge corpus and comparable performance to top-performing models on the Google Quanza paraphrase dataset.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture, which posits that a specific range of the fine structure constant is necessary for a given force to be relevant in a theory, has been proposed. However, the definition of this range is dependent on the convexity of the spectrum of charges in conformal field theories. The Charge Convexity Conjecture, which suggests that the spectrum of charges is convex, is a prerequisite for the validity of the Weak Gravity Conjecture. The purpose of this study is to examine the convexity of the spectrum of charges in Type IIB on $S^5$ and M5 on $S^1$, specifically in relation to the BPS states generated by single-string operators. The convexity of the spectrum of charges in these theories can be determined through the analysis of the central charges of the corresponding 2d conformal field theories obtained through a holographic duality. The study demonstrates that the spectrum of charges in these theories is non-convex, which is attributed to the presence of a specific boundary state known as the Casimir state. The convexity of the spectrum of charges can be restored in these theories by subtracting the contribution of the Casimir state from the corresponding 2d conformal field theories. The study also shows that the Casimir state contributes negatively to the central charge of the 2d conformal field theories, which results in a non-convex spectrum of charges. The study further demonstrates that the Casimir state

We propose a novel method to calculate the ground and excited states of a quantum system on a uniform grid using the quantum linear combination of time-fractional states method. This approach builds upon the Dirac equation and incorporates the Chebyshev discretization method for time-evolution. We demonstrate the accuracy of our method by solving a one-electron problem for the hydrogen atom and a two-electron problem for helium. Additionally, we present a technique to obtain excited states by a linear combination of ground and excited states obtained from different time-derivations. Furthermore, we introduce a method to obtain highly excited states with minimal spin contamination by applying the time-fractional operator for a short period of time, which effectively eliminates spin contamination.

We establish a condition characterized by a specific idempotent element which ensures F-rationality in Noetherian local rings of prime characteristic with an ideal of prime dimension greater than one. This condition supersedes and refines previous requirements from Testide, effectively generalizing his findings for graded rings to their ungraded counterparts. Furthermore, we provide a localized version of a result from Birkar, which in turn enables us to derive the proposed idempotent condition. Additionally, we define a right-left Noetherian ring in terms of the idempotent elements from which it can be constructed, and demonstrate its connection to F-regularity and its variants.

A proposed new modeling approach suggests that high orders of redispatch contracts could lead to negative consequences such as market instability and contract fulfillment issues. To examine this, we developed a mathematical model to analyze the effects of higher-order contracts on system stability and contract fulfillment in the electricity market. By applying variational inequality theory, we found that the proposed model results in a complex equilibrium state that may lead to market instability and contract nonfulfillment. Additionally, we found that the potential for market instability and contract nonfulfillment increases with higher-order contracts, especially in cases with significant inertia and response rates.

For a positive integer d, let's denote the set of polynomials of degree d over the rational numbers as Q[x]/(x^d - x). Given a monic polynomial P in this set, we'll consider the field extension generated by the values of P^k for k ranging from 1 to n, denoted as F_n. The Galois group of this extension, Gal(F_n/Q), is shown to be isomorphic to the k-th power of the Galois group of the base extension, Gal(F_1/Q^k), for any positive integer k that divides n. Furthermore, if n is a product of distinct prime numbers, the Galois group of F_n becomes isomorphic to the direct product of the Galois groups of the individual extensions F_p for each prime p dividing n.

This paper examines the production of a pair of Higgs bosons in association with two jets at next-to-leading order in perturbative QCD, focusing on the non-resonant case where the Higgs bosons decay into pairs of bottom quarks with low invariant masses. The study utilizes the NNPDF3.1 PDF set and is relevant for the Large Hadron Collider at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and luminosity of 300 fb^-1.

This study examines the production of a Standard Model Higgs boson in association with a Z boson at one-loop level, considering extended scalar sector models that incorporate a singlet scalar. We calculate one-loop corrections for this process, using a complex effective potential approach to incorporate the effects of strong electroweak symmetry breaking. Our calculations demonstrate that one-loop corrections can significantly impact the Higgsstrahlung process, particularly for certain scenarios where the 125 GeV Higgs resonance is not primarily composed of the Standard Model doublets. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of these corrections on the $S/$$b$ discrimination variable, finding that they can lead to a reduction in the expected signal-to-background ratio of up to 20% for certain scenarios, and that this ratio can be recovered through the addition of a jet veto.

Saturn's polar atmosphere exhibits a unique and intriguing phenomenon at its north pole, characterized by a large, warm vortex surrounding a persistent hexagonal shape. This discovery was made possible by the Saturnian north polar stratospheric cloud layer, which was revealed through infrared observations from the Cassini spacecraft. These findings indicate that the hexagon's stability is short-lived, lasting only about 20 Earth years, and that it is influenced by a sudden shift in the solar wind. Additionally, the hexagon's formation is attributed to a sudden change in Saturn's atmospheric rotation rate, which resulted from a massive disruption of the planet's atmospheric rotation. This study examines the global behavior of solutions to the Schrödinger equation under a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, either in a finite energy space or in an energy space with solutions of negative energy and bounded dispersion, depending on initial conditions. We demonstrate that solutions either disintegrate or form solitons. Additionally, we establish the existence of blow-up solutions with arbitrarily small amplitude and negative energy.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ has been extensively studied but its underlying causes remain unclear. To gain insight, we investigated the effect of surface termination on V$_2$O$_3$ films. Our findings indicate that the metal-insulator transition is influenced by the surface termination, with the metal phase stabilized when the surface is terminated with oxygen and the insulating phase when terminated with vanadium. This effect is attributed to the presence of a conducting surface layer at the metal phase and a localized, magnetic surface layer at the insulating phase. Our results demonstrate the significance of surface termination in the metal-insulator transition of V$_2$O$_3$ and highlight the need for consideration of this factor in future studies of this material system.

We investigate a quantum double dark-soliton state in the one-dimensional Bose Hubbard model and find that it can exhibit quasi-Bose-Einstein condensation in a finite number of sites. By applying a perturbation method, we analyze the dynamics of this state and find that quasi-Bose-Einstein condensation occurs in a finite region, leading to the formation of a quantum double dark-soliton state. We also study the effects of this state on the dynamics of a quantum dark-soliton state and find that they are similar, with the exception of a finite-size effect.

We develop a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle, extending the concept of linearising a Lie algebroid to a broader class of objects. This leads to the creation of a category whose morphisms are derived from algebroid morphisms, and whose objects include the sections of a graded bundle, now considered as graded connections.

This informal note outlines a formula for the absolute value of a certain expression related to orbital integrals of the algebraic torus in a local body of scalars, and also provides a context for the significance of this expression within the framework of the beyond-endoscopy approach.

The interaction between light and matter, which underlies various spectroscopic techniques, involves a wealth of phase information that has traditionally been disregarded due to the use of intensity-based measurement methods. This concept is particularly relevant in coherent Raman spectroscopy (CRS), specifically coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS), where the phase information of signals generated during the interaction of light with matter contains valuable molecular information. However, the phase information of CARS signals is subject to fluctuations that complicate the interpretation of the data. This research presents a novel approach to phase information analysis in CARS, utilizing a statistical method to extract the most probable phase information from a sample with known structure. The proposed method was tested using synthetic data and real-world data from a polystyrene sample, demonstrating its effectiveness in recovering the phase information and reconstructing the molecular structure.

Achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing requires error correcting codes that can withstand errors greater than a certain threshold without losing information. We demonstrate that quantum computers using any stabilizer code can accurately process information as long as the error rate is below a specific point, without this point being a continuous variable. This shows that codes like Shor's code can function properly if the error rate is low enough, without needing continuous stabilization. Additionally, we found that the error threshold for the toric code is 11.43%, which can be achieved with superconducting qubits using magnetic resonance.

Recent studies have shown that group VI elemental monolayers (such as sulfur, selenium, and tellurium) can be effectively functionalized with oxygen to possess unique topological properties. In this study, we investigate the effects of nitrogen functionalization on group VI monolayers. Our analysis reveals that the incorporation of nitrogen into these monolayers generates Dirac points and topological nodal lines, which can be stabilized in the sulfur and selenium monolayers, respectively. Notably, the tellurium monolayer exhibits topological nodal lines that can be transformed into Dirac points through applied strain. Our findings suggest that group VI monolayers functionalized with nitrogen have great potential for realizing exotic electronic properties.

This study presents a novel approach to upscaling permeability in fractured media, classifying fractures into two categories based on their conductivity. We introduce a new method to determine the effective permeability, applicable to both conductive and blocking fractures, and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to study the interplay between magnetic and superconducting orders in materials with strong spin-spin interactions. This approach applies to systems with both uniform and nonuniform magnetic orders, and can be used to analyze the effects of magnetic impurities on superconductivity. A specific study on CeIn$_3$ has revealed that the long-range triplet superconducting correlations are significantly influenced by the magnetic order, particularly in the presence of a particular type of magnetic domain. Furthermore, this phenomenon can be explained by considering the local magnetic moments in the material's unit cells, and can be described by a spin-triplet $d$-wave pairing model. This theoretical framework provides a foundation for understanding the complex interplay between magnetic and superconducting orders in heavy-fermion materials, and can be applied to other systems with strong spin-spin interactions.

When evaluating competing theories, Bayes factors provide a relative measure of their predictive accuracy. This study demonstrates an approach to compute Bayes factors for a specific class of models, specifically those that involve a linear transformation of a low-rank matrix in a high-dimensional space, as defined in equation 1. By leveraging a data augmentation algorithm, we derive an expression for the Bayes factor in equation 2, which can be efficiently computed using a single Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation. In chapter 2, we apply this approach to determine the minimum number of dimensions required for a low-rank matrix model, as outlined in equation 3. Furthermore, we extend this method to a generalized low-rank matrix model in equation 4 and utilize it to investigate a real-world dataset in chapter 3.

Discourse indicators like "by contrast" and "happily" convey the connections between sentences, which are often overlooked in language analysis. This study proposes a method to automatically identify and categorize these indicators in Arabic, French, and English, and uses them to classify sentence relationships. A machine learning algorithm is developed to predict these relationships from text without human intervention, and the results show that using discourse indicators improves accuracy.

We have demonstrated the creation of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond with a specific orientation, where a strong optical response to a particular laser wavelength exists at room temperature. This center typically only exhibits this response at very low temperatures. By using diamond with a high nitrogen content, we were able to increase the number of these centers by several orders of magnitude compared to previous methods. We found that the intensity of a specific optical phenomenon, radiative decay, can be significantly affected by temperature, and we were able to use this effect to enhance its intensity by over 10 times. This is particularly useful for ensembles of these centers, as it enables the creation of a strong optical response at room temperature.

The backpropagation algorithm, a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, enables efficient training of artificial neural networks. However, its widespread adoption in neuroscience is hindered by two significant issues: the need for a global credit assignment signal and the one-way information flow between neurons. We present an alternative training method that utilizes local, bidirectional synaptic connections, allowing for efficient credit assignment and precise weight updates. This new algorithm leverages the properties of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) to learn and generalize, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to a range of complex tasks, including supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. Our results show that this algorithm can learn and generalize, and we provide a theoretical framework explaining its behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this algorithm can learn at a rate comparable to backpropagation, and we explore its potential to explain the mechanisms underlying the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus.

Using a large-$p$ limit expansion, we re-examine a spin model on a triangular lattice inspired by the Heisenberg spin model, where the spin-$p$ representation is used. This investigation focuses on the $SU(3)$ version of the model, with spin set to $p=3$. By analyzing the triquadratic nature of the Hamiltonian, we find that a $SU(3)$ chiral liquid effective theory emerges at low energies. This theory can be understood as a weak-coupling perturbation of a $SU(3)$ Wess-Zumino-Witten model, with a specific pattern of symmetry breaking. We demonstrate that this effective theory exhibits a stable fixed point, and that this fixed point can be reached through a phase transition from the high-energy regime.

A new approach has been implemented to generate and analyze the ground states of an electron gas confined by a harmonic potential. By applying the Kohn-Sham method within the local density approximation, we created a dataset of ground states for various electron numbers and confinement strengths. We then applied the diagonalization quantum Monte Carlo method to sample and analyze these ground states. The results show that the ground states can be accurately classified based on the spin state and orbital angular momentum content. The analysis also reveals that the electron gas exhibits a robust tendency towards pairing in the orbital angular momentum states with $l\geq2$.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior in complex systems is not absolute, as certain states can possess elements of both order and disorder. Recent studies have identified periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic dynamics in systems like the Kuramoto model, log-gamma sub-Shifted process, and Hénon map. To better understand these functional states, researchers propose a new framework that uses multifunctional analysis to characterize their structures and dynamics. Within this framework, they develop a metric to measure the complexity of systems and apply it to study the coexistence of order and disorder in the mentioned systems, as well as a spatially extended system known as the Kuramoto-Gross-Bogoliubov model.

We investigate the global landscape of the Riemannian quotient optimization problem resulting from Burer-Monteiro factorization, specifically for a matrix whose entries are constrained to non-negativity, for a matrix whose entries are unconstrained, and for a matrix whose entries follow a Bernoulli distribution. The associated objective function is defined on a manifold of positive semidefinite matrices under Euclidean, symmetric Euclidean, and Grassmannian geometries, respectively. Our analysis reveals three distinct regions within the landscape: a neighborhood of local minimizers where the Hessian is positive definite, a region characterized by the presence of local maximizers with negative curvature, and a region where the curvature is positive but may not be definite. Our findings are relevant to the convergence analysis of optimization algorithms applied to the BM factorized formulation.

A graph's edge coloring is strong if adjacent edges are assigned different colors, and for every edge, there's a vertex for which the edges incident to that vertex have distinct colors. This concept combines ideas from edge and vertex coloring. We present a new approach using the precoloring method, where certain edges are assigned specific colors. Our goal is to color all remaining edges while adhering to the strong criterion. We examine this problem for various scenarios, including when some edges are precolored and when no edges have preassigned colors.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$.

High-energy particles, whose masses exceed the TeV range, are difficult to study directly. However, the sensitivity of next-generation gravitational wave detectors can help by providing a new way to constrain these particles through the decay process that produces gravitational waves. In this study, we examine the potential of using gravitational wave observations to limit the production of heavy particles in various new physics scenarios, including composite Higgs, extra-dimension, and supersymmetry. We also investigate the effectiveness of future gravitational wave experiments in discovering or ruling out these physics scenarios at the TeV range.

Our research reveals that a swimmer's geometry plays a crucial role in determining its swimming speed in viscoelastic fluids, with its speed being significantly higher in these fluids than in non-Newtonian fluids. To explore this phenomenon, we analyze two types of swimmers: a helical swimmer and a double-swimmer, both in dilute polymer solutions and in cross-linked polymer systems. Our findings show that the swimmer's speed is greatly enhanced in viscoelastic fluids, with this enhancement being more pronounced in cross-linked polymer systems. Notably, we find that the swimmer's speed is highly sensitive to the fluid's elasticity in these systems. To understand this sensitivity, we develop a simplified model that highlights the importance of the swimmer's geometry in determining its speed in viscoelastic fluids.

We investigate the impact of social learning algorithms on the convergence to a Nash Equilibrium (NE) in a large class of games with multiple equilibria, and find that they can achieve nearly optimal learning rates. This finding is particularly significant as many games exhibit multiple equilibria, a scenario for which learning algorithms' convergence to NE has not been extensively studied. In contrast, numerous studies have demonstrated the rapid convergence to NE in games with a single equilibrium or in scenarios where players' actions are restricted. Notably, our analysis reveals that social learning algorithms achieve a learning rate of $\sqrt{T}$, which is comparable to the $\sqrt{T}$ learning rate achieved by individual learning algorithms in games with a single equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the average regret of social learning algorithms of $O(\sqrt{T})$, which is the first known bound for learning algorithms in games with multiple NE.

This research paper proposes an approach to enhance information security through an advanced approach called Advanced Security Ontology (ASO). The ASO system utilizes a semantic framework that leverages Web-based technologies to provide a comprehensive and adaptable security infrastructure. The ASO framework is comprised of two primary modules: the Security Knowledge Base (SKB) and the Security Rule Engine (SRE). The SKB module aggregates and manages a vast amount of security-related data from diverse sources, including databases, APIs, and file systems. In contrast, the SRE module is responsible for analyzing the ontology and generating security rules to protect against potential threats. The ASO system is designed to be highly extensible, allowing it to seamlessly integrate with existing security systems via Web Services. The system's adaptability is further ensured through the use of WS-Policy, which enables it to dynamically adjust security configurations in response to changing conditions. The ASO framework has been successfully implemented and tested on a prototype system, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting and mitigating security threats.

We investigate a social dynamics model that includes both Ising and Heisenberg agents, with their interactions represented by local update rules inspired by Glauber's algorithm. The model is applied to a square lattice, and we analyze the impact of the concentration of Ising agents on the ordering of the system for both finite and zero temperatures. Our findings indicate that a significant proportion of Ising agents can lead to ferromagnetic ordering at both high and low temperatures, while a higher concentration of Heisenberg agents is required to achieve similar ordering.

The COVID-19 pandemic emphasizes the significance of understanding how respiratory pathogens spread through evaporation of contaminated droplets in various environments. To investigate this, we developed a comprehensive model that considers the effects of temperature, humidity, and air flow on the evaporation of droplets of varying sizes. Our results reveal that the presence of stokes layers has a substantial impact on the evaporation of droplets, especially in environments with low humidity and moderate temperatures. Furthermore, we found that the model we developed is highly accurate in predicting the evaporation of droplets, even in conditions where traditional models may fail. To facilitate practical applications, we created a simplified model that can efficiently estimate the evaporation of droplets in any given environment.
